subject: literature
passage: The novelist Thomas Allard set his books of the 1860s and 1870s among farming families and wrote their speech in dialect spelling, dropping letters and respelling words to capture local pronunciation. In editions published after 1885, much of this spelling was replaced with standard forms. Literary scholar Hannah Brooks argues that Allard himself made the change, yielding to reviewers who had complained that the dialect made his books tiring to read, rather than the publisher imposing it without his knowledge, as some have assumed.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brooks's argument?

choices.A: The editions published after 1885 also corrected a number of printing errors found in the early editions.
choices.B: Allard's own copies of the early editions survive with the dialect spellings crossed out and standard spellings written in beside them in his handwriting.
choices.C: Allard's publisher issued the later editions in a cheaper format aimed at a wider public.
choices.D: Reviews of the early editions praised the dialect speech as the most lifelike feature of the books.

explanation.why: Brooks claims the author made the change himself. The most direct evidence would show Allard revising the dialect in his own hand. His marked-up copies with standard spellings written in do exactly that, and they rule out the idea that the publisher acted without his knowledge.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Correcting printing errors is routine and does not show who changed the dialect spelling.
explanation.B: Correct. Revisions in Allard's own handwriting show that he, not the publisher alone, made the change.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The format of the later editions does not reveal who decided to alter the spelling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Reviewers praising the dialect runs against the premise that complaints prompted the change, so this does not support Brooks.
